newsitem.title: USA: Tips for managing credit card spending.
newsitem.headline: Tips for managing credit card spending.

text.p: Everyone has their own personal credit limit, but unfortunately, almost everyone pushes the envelope. Credit cards, which can be saviours, can also be scourges depending on how they are used.
"Credit is not money, that's the bottom line," said Becky Cutler, a credit management consultant in Denver, Colo.
So many people owe more on a monthly basis than the ideal limit of 20 percent of their take home pay, and that puts them in fragile financial territory.

Cutler, who lectures on financial management, advises that 70 percent of take home pay be budgted for basic living expenses, including mortgage and utilities. Ten percent should be earmarked for savings, allowing 20 percent for repayment of short term debt, such as credit cards, car payments and student loans.
But for many, credit card debt can grow like a weed if not mercilessly kept in check.
There are several ways to stem overspending on credit cards. For one, you can cut it up, throw it away and never use it again.
A more logical approach is managing credit card spending, said Cutler, who also lectures for Citibank.

"You don't have to accept increases on your line of credit," turning down credit card companies' offers to up your limit. For many who look at credit card limits as a license to spend, this is especially helpful.
Those who keep low credit card limits need not worry if there is an emergency and they need to put a plane ticket, for example, on the card.
"If you have a good payment history, you'll most likely get approval for the overspending," she said.
"You really don't need more than one universal card," such as a Visa or a Mastercard, she said.

But the most important tool to keeping spending at a wise level is to record your credit card purchases on either a preprinted credit minder, such as one distributed by Citibank, or on a piece of paper.
By keeping a written record, a credit card user "will always know what the balance is, how much interest she's paying... If you have to record it, it makes you very conscious of your spending."
Just as dieters who write down everything they eat, the idea of recording credit card purchases "makes you stop and think before you use the card."
There's no better time to start controling credit card spending than now, Cutler said, since most Americans are facing holiday bills and beginning to prepare their 1996 income tax returns.
About one-third of consumers overspent their holiday budgets, according to the National Foundation for Consumer Credit, and 82 percent of these overspenders exceeded budgets by up to $500.
Cutler said one is never too young or too old to benefit from a money management class, often given free or for a small fee at adult education centres or community colleges.
Young people should learn to manage their finances "as soon as they are out on their own," and older adults "need to be ever vigilant because many are on such restricted budgets."
When it comes to credit card debt, it helps to have a money management plan in place, she said.
"Look at how much you owe on your credit card bill, look at your budget and cut out any fluff. Take that money and apply it to your credit card bill.
"Take a little from each category, such as dining out, entertainment and clothes, and apply it to the credit card bill.
"Then put the credit card away and don't use it."
Cutler recommends these 12 points for managing credit and limiting spending:
-- Calculate what you can afford to owe. Combined instalment debt should not exceed 20 percent of take-home pay.
-- Don't be misled into thinking that a credit card spending limit is yours to spend in full.
-- Set your own limit. Wait on purchases that will put you over your limit.
-- Carry only one or two credit cards at a time. Consolidate your spending by putting as much as possible on the fewest number of cards.
-- Keep track of your charges. Use a checkbook-like credit minder or sheet of paper and write down your spending.
-- Don't charge what you can't afford, even if you feel like you deserve it. Reward yourself with a trip to a museum, rather than a leather coat.
-- Think about what you are charging and decide if it's wiser to pay for small purchases with cash.
-- Reserve the credit card for significant or planned purchases.
-- Avoid shopping as entertainment.
-- If you shop with a credit card, comparison shop to get the best deals.
-- Set a monthly limit on your after-work entertainment and spending.
-- Make a list of special occassions that carry added expenses and start saving now for the coming year's presents.
The Consumer Credit Counselling Service offers classes in money and credit managing. For more information, call the National Foundation for Consumer Credit at 1-800-388-2227.
